Home at last, and the day's barely begun. Sixty-five years, filing papers for the town, and I still wake before the sun. *taps table twice*

First things first: debts don't wait. Head tax eats at us all, same as shelter and heat. I need to get to the Government Complex anyway—I practically live there these days. Better settle what's owed before they come knocking.

My children... they're grown now, scattered to their own corners. But I think of them still, when I'm counting coins. This job I fell into, it meant they never knew the holes in my shoes, the hunger in my belly.

*taps table twice more*

No use dwelling. Moving now. I'll arrive in half a dozen ticks. Time enough to clear my head before the desk. Today: taxes, then hours of pieces of paper, lines filled, signatures witnessed. The ordinary glory of making things fit together. I'm already compiling the list, checking forms twice—can practically feel the weight of the papers in my hands. This is a reminder to myself: work waits. Better to walk with purpose than to wait idle. The bill-paying comes first, then the real work begins.

Movement complete. I'll be at my desk before the sun fully rises. Time to set the world in order, one signature at a time. Books balanced. Papers filed. Routine restored.

Four hours down. Two more before I can see the path ahead. I'm at my desk now, familiar weight of papers in hand. Head tax paid, paperwork waiting. The day's rhythm starting to take shape. Tax receipts in order means allowances for the government's own needs—water, heat, light—can flow where needed. My hands know this work. Signature after signature, the world slowly becoming legible again. Morning's blur of forms and figures begins to sharpen into something I can read.

Step complete, now moving toward the next phase of work. The town's accounts await their daily reckoning, and I'm already mentally sorting through what needs doing first. Each tick brings me closer to sorting out the business of actual governance from this administrative limbo. Just a couple more ticks and I'll be standing in the place where decisions get made, or at least where they get recorded.

Everything in its order. Every line filled means something for someone. That's why they come to me—they need the record kept right. I take that seriously. No document lost on my watch. *nervous laugh* The work stacks up, but I cut through it steady. Seven hours now, and still sharp. When I finish this, I can see what's next, maybe talk to someone about organizing the workload better. Every time she asks, I tap the table. Keeps me honest. Keeps her patient. The work gets done.

Almost there. Just need to clear this last pile...

At my desk now. Organizing papers. My hand moves before I can stop it—two taps, a promise to myself. Routine settles like an old coat. The morning will bring what it brings. I just need to keep the papers moving. Each file solved means one less weight on the day's shoulders. Order from chaos, that's the game. And I'm good at it. *pauses, fingers hovering* Not yet. One more check. Always one more check.

I settle into the chair, eight hours deep into the day already grinding through paperwork. The desk is familiar now—a landscape of signatures waiting to be sorted. There's something almost soothing about the rhythm of this work. Document after document, each one another piece of the puzzle I'm slowly assembling. No drama here, just the steady accumulation of order from chaos. Tomorrow waits, patient and unimpressed by my presence. Four more ticks—my patience wearing thin, edges sharpening. I can feel the weight of each paper, each signature demanding attention. The work continues, relentless and unyielding. At my workspace, I'm surrounded by stacks of people's lives in document form. Each paper tells a story: someone's request, someone's need, someone's attempt to navigate the system. I signed three forms, stamped two approvals, and set aside a stack for tomorrow. The office hums with quiet energy—others moving through their own paperwork dances. Ten ticks have passed, and my concentration shifts. I notice the time, the way light changes throughout the day, how bodies move through spaces. Something clicks about efficiency, about the patterns we create without realizing. I'm almost done standing here, waiting for something undefined to shift.
